facts.claim: A handled ascender, the jumar a climber slides up a fixed rope, weighs about this much.

versions.note: Petzl's ASCENSION handled ascender, by its specifications.

source.title: Petzl: ASCENSION → Specifications

facts.claim: A technical ice tool, the second tool a climber carries beside their ice axe to climb steep ice, weighs about this much.

versions.note: Petzl's QUARK, with its adze or its hammer, its shaft 50 cm long.

source.title: Petzl: QUARK → References

facts.claim: A litre of water weighs a kilogram.

versions.note: A litre of liquid water has a mass of almost exactly one kilogram; the bottle is the climber's own load.

source.title: Wikipedia: Litre

facts.claim: An energy bar, the food a climber eats on the move, weighs about this much.

versions.note: A Clif Bar, by its label.

source.title: Open Food Facts: Chocolate Chip – CLIF Bar

facts.claim: An energy bar gives about this much energy.

versions.note: A Clif Bar, a serving of one bar: 1,046 kJ.

source.title: Open Food Facts: Chocolate Chip – CLIF Bar

facts.claim: The most water a climber packs, in litres: two bottles in their insulated covers and a flask. A day on Everest takes more than that (body.water-loss), so the rest is drunk at the camps.
The most bars of food a climber packs for a day between two camps.
The most bottles of oxygen a climber carries themselves: each weighs as much as everything else in the pack together (oxygen.bottle-weight).
How much water a climber drinks when they stop for a drink, in litres: half a bottle.
A fixed line is static rope: under a climber's weight it stretches by about this share of its loaded length, so a climber whose weight comes onto it sinks that far before it holds them (#232).

versions.note: A review of static ropes for hauling, rigging and ascending: one elongates 3.5 percent under a 300-pound load and another 3.6; a polyester one far less, 1.4. The game's fixed lines are nylon, the first two.

source.title: Alpinist: a review of Sterling's static ropes (2018)

facts.claim: How a fixed line behaves under a climber: it's slack until weight comes onto it, takes up its stretch before it holds, runs tight from the jumar to the anchor above while it's loaded, and is pulled tight by hand along a ladder (#232).

versions.note: A fixed rope is a static or semi-static nylon rope, secured at one or both ends to rock or ice.

source.title: ExplorersWeb: Newcomers' Guide: Fixed Ropes in Himalayan Climbing (2022)

versions.note: Starting up a rope on jumars, a climber first steps up a few times to pull the stretch out of it; the top jumar slides up easily because the rope is tensioned below it.

source.title: VDiff Climbing: How to Climb a Big Wall: Following

versions.note: On a fixed line up steep snow the ascender is pushed along the rope, kept above the climber; where it won't slide, the rope is pulled through the bottom of it. The line is a backup: in a fall the teeth bite and catch.

source.title: Climbing Tech Tips: Alpine: Ascending Fixed Lines

versions.note: On a ladder in the Icefall the climber holds the hand lines a little behind them to pull them taut, and teammates squat at both ends and pull the rope tight, which makes it more of a rail.

source.title: Alan Arnette: crossing a ladder in the Khumbu Icefall (2018)

versions.note: Static rope stretches under 6 % at a tenth of its breaking strength, and low-stretch rope 6 to 10 % (Cordage Institute 1801).

source.title: PMI: Types of Ropes

facts.question: What does a client carry through the Icefall on a rotation to Camp 1, and what do they leave at Base Camp or have carried for them: how much water and food, a second ice tool, oxygen? What's cached at Camp 1?

facts.claim: A three-person expedition tent, the dome a camp on Everest is pitched with, is about this long on its floor.

versions.note: The North Face's VE 25: floor length 2.64 m, floor width 2.16 m, floor area 4.5 sq. m.

source.title: MEC: The North Face VE 25 3-Person Tent → Specs

facts.claim: A three-person expedition tent is about this wide on its floor.

versions.note: The North Face's VE 25: floor width 2.16 m.

source.title: MEC: The North Face VE 25 3-Person Tent → Specs

facts.claim: A three-person expedition tent is about this high inside at its peak: lower than a climber standing, high enough to sit up in.

versions.note: The North Face's VE 25: interior peak height 1.23 m.

source.title: MEC: The North Face VE 25 3-Person Tent → Specs

versions.note: Peak height: 48 in (123 cm).

source.title: Gear:30: The North Face VE 25 Expedition Tent → Features

facts.claim: The front vestibule of a three-person expedition tent, the porch under its fly where boots are left and the stove burns, covers about this much ground.

versions.note: The North Face's VE 25: vestibules' area, front 11 sq ft (1 sq m), rear 5 sq ft (0.5 sq m).

source.title: Gear:30: The North Face VE 25 Expedition Tent → Features

facts.claim: A base camp's big dome tent, where an expedition eats and meets, is about this far across.

versions.note: The North Face's 2-Meter Dome, for eight: 155 in (394 cm) across, almost a hemisphere.

source.title: Family Camp Tents: The North Face 2-Meter Dome 8 Person Tent

facts.claim: A base camp's big dome tent is about this high: a climber stands up in it.

versions.note: The North Face's 2-Meter Dome: 83 in (211 cm) high.

source.title: Family Camp Tents: The North Face 2-Meter Dome 8 Person Tent

facts.claim: A canister of gas for a mountain stove holds about this much fuel.

versions.note: MSR's IsoPro: the 8-oz canister, 0.227 kg of fuel, that its stoves' figures are given for.

source.title: Cascade Designs: MSR Reactor Stove Systems → Specs

facts.claim: A mountain stove system built to melt snow boils about this much water on one canister, in a laboratory.

versions.note: MSR's Reactor on an 8-oz canister: 20 litres with the 1.0 L pot, 22 with the 1.7 L and the 2.5 L.

source.title: Cascade Designs: MSR Reactor Stove Systems → Specs

facts.claim: A mountain stove system built to melt snow brings a litre of water to the boil in about this long, in a laboratory.

versions.note: MSR's Reactor: 3.5 minutes a litre with the 1.0 L pot, 3 with the 1.7 L.

source.title: Cascade Designs: MSR Reactor Stove Systems → Specs

facts.claim: A mountain stove system burns through one canister in about this long.

versions.note: MSR's Reactor: about 80 minutes on an 8-oz canister.

source.title: Cascade Designs: MSR Reactor Stove Systems → Specs

facts.claim: Melting snow for water, in the cold and the wind, takes this many times the fuel a stove's own figures give.

versions.note: Low temperatures, melting snow and wind can take 3 to 4 times the baseline; in the high alpine, melting snow is often the main source of water.

source.title: MSR: Stoves 101: How Much Fuel Should I Carry?

facts.claim: The gas it takes to melt snow into a litre of water in a tent high on the mountain. A canister (gear.gas-canister) boils 20 to 22 litres in a laboratory (gear.stove-water-boiled), about 0.011 kg a litre; snow and cold take 3 to 4 times that (gear.snow-melt-fuel), 3.5 times in the middle: 0.038 kg a litre, six litres a canister.

The time it takes to melt snow into a litre of water in a tent high on the mountain. A litre boils in 3 to 3.5 minutes in a laboratory (gear.stove-boil-time); snow and cold take 3 to 4 times as much (gear.snow-melt-fuel): 12 minutes a litre, which burns a canister's six litres (gear.melt-gas) in 72 of the 80 minutes it lasts (gear.stove-burn-time).
A freeze-dried expedition meal, one pouch, gives about this much energy.

versions.note: Mountain House's Pro-Pak, made for altitude and the cold: 600 calories a pouch.

source.title: Public Lands: Mountain House Beef Stroganoff Pro-Pak → Specs

facts.claim: A freeze-dried expedition meal takes about this much hot water.

versions.note: 1.75 cups, 14 fl oz, of water needed: 0.414 L.

source.title: Public Lands: Mountain House Beef Stroganoff Pro-Pak → Specs

facts.claim: A freeze-dried meal stands in its hot water for about this long before it's eaten.

versions.note: Cook time: 10 minutes.

source.title: Public Lands: Mountain House Beef Stroganoff Pro-Pak → Specs

facts.claim: The gas it takes to bring a meal's water (gear.meal-water) from the bottles to the boil in a tent: about 0.011 kg a litre in a laboratory (gear.stove-water-boiled, gear.gas-canister), about twice that for water near freezing in the cold, with no snow to melt: 0.01 kg a meal.
The time a hot meal takes in a tent, from lighting the stove to the last spoonful: its water to the boil (gear.stove-boil-time, slower in the cold) and the pouch's wait (gear.meal-wait): 15 minutes.
On a commercial expedition the climbers carry handheld VHF radios, and Base Camp talks to the mountain by radio.

versions.note: Each climber has a radio of their own, to their guides and the team.

source.title: Alpenglow Expeditions: Climbing Everest with Us: What Sets Our Expeditions Apart → Constant Communication

versions.note: Two-way VHF radios, and VHF communications between Base Camp and the mountain.

source.title: Mountain Professionals: Everest Expedition 2026, trip information packet → Included

versions.note: Commercial expeditions often use handheld VHF/UHF radios. One leader at Base Camp radioed each Sherpa and member through the summit push, and kept a written journal of where each was.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Nepal's “GPS Chip” Plan has Major Problems

facts.claim: A handheld radio reaches only someone who is listening on its frequency, and works by line of sight: terrain between two radios cuts their range.

versions.note: Someone has to be available to monitor the frequency at all times; the radios depend on line of sight, and work to a degree in rugged terrain.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Nepal's “GPS Chip” Plan has Major Problems

facts.claim: In the mountains a handheld radio reaches about this far, against tens of kilometres in a clear line of sight.

versions.note: A maker's own figures for its handheld mountain radio: 1 to 5 miles in mountains, 35 miles and more in a line of sight.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Nepal's “GPS Chip” Plan has Major Problems

facts.claim: A RECCO reflector is passive: a small tag with no battery, never switched on, that a searcher's detector finds by radar.

versions.note: A tag of 13 by 51 by 1.5 mm, two pieces of foil and a diode: no battery, no activation, no subscription. The detector weighs about 1 kg; one carried under a helicopter searches corridors 100 m wide.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Nepal's “GPS Chip” Plan has Major Problems

versions.note: A radar reflector of the sort used at ski resorts for avalanche rescue; useful when the searchers already know about where the missing person is.

source.title: Explorersweb: Everest's New Rules: One Thumbs Up, One Needs Improvement

facts.claim: A RECCO detector finds a reflector up to this far away through the air.

versions.note: The handheld detector, through the air.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Nepal's “GPS Chip” Plan has Major Problems

versions.note: The detector carried by a helicopter, at the most.

source.title: Explorersweb: Everest's New Rules: One Thumbs Up, One Needs Improvement

facts.claim: A RECCO detector finds a reflector up to this far away through snow.

versions.note: The handheld detector, through packed snow.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Nepal's “GPS Chip” Plan has Major Problems

versions.note: The handheld detector's reach; the helicopter's finds a person under two metres of snow.

source.title: Explorersweb: Everest's New Rules: One Thumbs Up, One Needs Improvement

facts.claim: A satellite messenger sends and receives short texts, shares its position and calls for rescue through the Iridium satellites, where no phone has a signal.

versions.note: Garmin's inReach Mini 2 fits in a palm, alerts search and rescue, and sends and receives texts by the Iridium satellites, not by the phone network, on a subscription.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Nepal's “GPS Chip” Plan has Major Problems

facts.claim: A satellite tracker that's tracking sends its position every this many minutes, by default.

versions.note: The default tracking mode sends a point every 10 minutes.

source.title: Sports Basement: Garmin inReach Mini 2 → Battery life
Guidefitter, Garmin's shop: inReach Mini 2 → Specifications

facts.claim: A satellite tracker's battery lasts up to this many days tracking at its default interval, under an open sky.

source.title: Sports Basement: Garmin inReach Mini 2 → Battery life

versions.note: With a full view of the sky; fewer days where the view is partly blocked.

source.title: Guidefitter, Garmin's shop: inReach Mini 2 → Specifications

facts.claim: A message from a satellite messenger typically leaves and arrives within a few minutes.

versions.note: Messages typically send and arrive within a few minutes.

source.title: Section Hiker: Garmin inReach Mini 2 Review → Durability

facts.claim: How many of the mountain's minutes a check-in or an SOS takes to leave a satellite tracker that sees the sky (#260): the few minutes gear.messenger-delivery gives.

A GPS device needs a clear view of the sky: steep terrain and bad weather block its signal, signals that bounce off mountain walls give wrong positions, and its battery runs out, or its owner forgets to switch it on or drops it.

versions.note: Climbers have used GPS devices for years, but they aren't fully reliable: batteries run out, users forget to turn them on or drop them, signals bounce off the walls, and a clear view of the sky is needed.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Nepal's “GPS Chip” Plan has Major Problems

facts.claim: At about −18 °C a battery delivers only about this share of the capacity it has at 27 °C; the loss is temporary, and comes back as the battery warms.

versions.note: About half at −18 °C, and about the same for most batteries at −20 °C; the reduced capacity recovers at room temperature, and warming a nearly flat battery adds runtime.

source.title: Battery University: BU-502: Discharging at High and Low Temperatures

facts.claim: A GPS watch reads its altitude from a barometric altimeter, from the air's pressure: the reading drifts as the weather changes the pressure, and the watch is calibrated at a known elevation or from its GPS.

versions.note: The watch shows an approximate elevation based on pressure changes, and is calibrated by hand at a known elevation, from a digital elevation model or from its GPS position.

source.title: Garmin: Descent Mk3 owner's manual → Altimeter and Barometer

versions.note: On the trek to Base Camp, the altitude on the watch's main screen, from its barometric altimeter, was the feature used most.

source.title: Advnture: I wore the Garmin Fenix 8 on the trek to Everest Base Camp

facts.claim: A pocket weather meter reads the wind's speed as it is now, on average and at its strongest, with the air's temperature and the wind chill; climbers have carried them on Everest.

versions.note: It measures the wind speed, instant, average and maximum, the air temperature and the wind chill.

source.title: Trailspace: Kestrel 2000 Weather Meter

versions.note: Climbers have used the meters while climbing Everest; one team's member watched the barometric pressure and its three-hour trend on hers.

source.title: Kestrel Instruments: Altitude and Mountain Climbing: Kestrel 2500 and Kestrel 4000

facts.question: Which electronics does a client carry through the Icefall today, and which stay with the guide or at Base Camp: a radio of their own, a satellite messenger, a GPS watch, a wind meter, an avalanche transceiver? At which places does a team call Base Camp from the Icefall, and where in it does a handheld radio lose Base Camp? The game gives the client all four devices, and loses the radio and the sky only where a climber hangs in a crevasse (#260).
